subjective.question: Define performance management. How is performance management different from performance appraisal?
subjective.answer: Performance management is a systematic process for improving organizational performance by developing the performance of individuals and teams. It is a means of getting better results by understanding and managing performance within an agreed framework of planned goals, standards and competency requirements. It covers setting work goals, determining performance standards, assigning and evaluating work, providing feedback, determining training and development needs and distributing rewards. Performance appraisal, on the other hand, is only a review of an employee's performance over a period of time. Appraisal is just one phase of the performance management system, so the two terms should not be used interchangeably.

subjective.question: Explain the underlying theories on which the concept of performance management is based.
subjective.answer: Three theories underlie performance management. (1) Goal theory (Latham and Locke, 1979) highlights four mechanisms connecting goals to performance outcomes: goals direct attention to priorities, stimulate effort, challenge people to bring their knowledge and skills to bear, and the more challenging the goal, the more people draw on their full repertoire of skills. (2) Control theory focuses on feedback as a means of shaping behavior: as people receive feedback they appreciate the discrepancy between what they are doing and what they are expected to do and take corrective action. (3) Social cognitive theory (Bandura, 1986) is based on self-efficacy: what people believe they can or cannot do powerfully impacts their performance, so developing positive self-belief in employees is an important performance management objective.

subjective.question: Discuss the purposes served by a performance management system in an organization.
subjective.answer: A performance management system serves several purposes. Strategic purpose: it links the organization's goals with individual goals, reinforcing behaviors consistent with the attainment of organizational goals. Administrative purpose: it is a source of valid and useful information for decisions about employees, including salary adjustments, promotions, retention or termination, recognition of superior performance, identification of poor performers, layoffs and merit increases. Organizational maintenance purpose: it yields information about skills, abilities, promotional potential and assignment histories for workforce planning, assessing future training needs and evaluating the effectiveness of HR interventions. Documentation purpose: it yields data to assess the predictive accuracy of newly proposed selection instruments and to support administrative decisions, which is especially useful in litigation. In addition, PMS serves developmental and communication purposes by identifying training needs and improving communication between employees and managers.

subjective.question: Explain the impact of a performance management system on employees, managers and the organization.
subjective.answer: For employees, PMS communicates performance expectations in the form of goals and standards; employees put in effort to meet them, which helps identify their performance gaps, and a transparent system with equity in reward distribution develops satisfaction, motivation and hard work. It answers the employees' questions: what is expected of me, how am I doing, and what does it mean for me. For managers and supervisors, PMS provides information about the competence level of employees, helps them communicate expectations accurately, differentiate poor and high performers, and coach employees to improve performance. For the organization, PMS attains organizational goals through improved individual and collective performance by fulfilling strategic, administrative, organizational maintenance and documentation purposes.

subjective.question: Differentiate between monetary and non-monetary rewards, giving examples of each.
subjective.answer: Monetary rewards are financial in nature and include basic pay, contingency pay, commission, incentives, pension and gratuity. Non-monetary rewards are non-financial and include recognition, employment security, challenging work, growth opportunities, personal relationships at work and autonomy. An effective reward system links all reward elements together and treats them as an integrated and coherent whole so that employees remain motivated for improved performance.

subjective.question: Which contextual factors should be considered while developing an effective reward system?
subjective.answer: Internal factors: (1) Organizational culture - the core values of the organization determine the criteria used in reviewing performance and rewarding people. (2) Business of the organization - manufacturing versus service, profit versus non-profit and public versus private organizations vary in criteria; for example piece-rate pay plans are used in manufacturing, skill-based plans are preferable in the service industry, and public organizations tend to offer fixed salaries. (3) Technology - new technology brings system and procedural changes requiring different skills and a variety of rewards. (4) Organizational people - their knowledge, skills and attitudes (KSAs) require customized guidance, motivation and rewards. External factors include competitive pressure, globalization (diverse workforce, inflation rates, hardship and security conditions of the locality), demographic patterns (age, gender, education, which influence pensions, medical allowances and flexible timing), and employment legislations (minimum wage rates and allowances set by government and regulatory bodies).

subjective.question: Enlist and briefly explain the characteristics of an ideal performance management system.
subjective.answer: An ideal PMS should be: (1) Congruent with strategy - aligned with the business strategy and supporting strategic goals. (2) Thorough - all employees appraised for the entire review period against every major job responsibility, with proper feedback. (3) Practical - easy to understand, easy to implement and cost-effective. (4) Meaningful - standards relevant to the job, evaluating only outcomes under the employee's control. (5) Specific - detailed guidance about expectations, goals, evaluation criteria and rewards. (6) Able to identify effective and ineffective performance - distinguishing high, average and low performers. (7) Reliable - consistent evaluation regardless of the supervisor. (8) Valid - includes all relevant performance dimensions and is not contaminated by non-human factors. (9) Fair and acceptable - based on distributive and procedural justice. (10) Inclusive - incorporates employee suggestions and concerns. (11) Open - standards and feedback open to everyone. (12) Correctable - appeal processes exist to challenge unjust evaluations. (13) Standardized - performance evaluated consistently across people and time. (14) Ethical - free of self-interest and bias, and protective of employee privacy.

subjective.question: Explain distributive justice and procedural justice as criteria of fairness in a PMS.
subjective.answer: Fairness of a PMS is based on two criteria. Distributive justice is the perception about the evaluation rating with respect to the work performed and the reward relative to the performance evaluation, in comparison to other employees within or outside the organization; if the distribution of rewards is perceived to be based on each employee's evaluation rating, the PMS is fair in distributive terms. Procedural justice is based on the procedures applied to evaluate performance and allocate rewards accordingly; if the evaluation and reward allocation procedure is perceived as equitable by employees, the PMS is considered fair in terms of procedures, and employees show acceptance of the system.

subjective.question: How is the performance management system integrated with other functions of HRM?
subjective.answer: PMS is a major component of HRM and is highly interdependent with other HRM functions. Training and development: information gathered through performance appraisals identifies the knowledge, skills and attitudes (KSAs) required by employees, so PMS feedback serves as a source of training need analysis (TNA), on the basis of which effective training and development is planned. Compensation management: this function is initiated after the completion of PMS; PMS provides information on employee performance and goal attainment, while compensation management rewards employees on their performance, ensuring transparent allocation of rewards. Human resource planning: HRP aligns the human resource with the organization's strategic plans and needs an in-depth analysis of the existing human resource in terms of KSAs, capabilities and talents, which PMS provides; on this basis the organization forecasts HR demand, to be met through training and development internally or through recruitment and selection externally.

subjective.question: What are the prerequisites of a performance management system? Why are they important?
subjective.answer: The two major prerequisites of PMS are knowledge of the organization's mission and knowledge of the job to be assessed. Knowledge of the organization's vision, mission and objectives is necessary to align job activities so that organizational goals can be met efficiently and effectively; if this link is weak, the organization can never achieve its performance goals regardless of the efforts, motivation and competencies of employees, and a PMS initiated with ambiguous mission and goals remains ineffective. Knowledge of the job means being well informed about the activities, responsibilities and competencies involved in performing the job; this is obtained through job analysis, from which the job description, job specification and job evaluation are extracted. Only when the mission is clearly defined and the job is described in detail can PMS be initiated effectively.

subjective.question: What is performance planning? Describe its components.
subjective.answer: Performance planning is the phase of PMS in which managers, supervisors and subordinates collaborate to discuss and agree upon the performance criteria, including results, behaviors and development plans. (1) Results/outcomes: this describes what needs to be achieved by the employee; it involves consensus on objectives and accountabilities, information extracted from the job description, measurable outcomes, and performance standards against which performance is evaluated. (2) Behaviors: where external factors strongly impact results, or the nature of the job depends on behavior (for example sales jobs), performance is evaluated on the basis of displayed behaviors, i.e., the employee's competencies and KSAs. (3) Development plans: evaluation should also meet development needs; performance gaps are identified through result-based criteria and addressed for improvement, while behavior-based evaluation defines the employee's capacity to learn and develop, so individual development leads to organizational development.

subjective.question: What is job analysis? State the steps involved in conducting a job analysis.
subjective.answer: Job analysis is the procedure through which an organization determines the duties of its positions and the characteristics of the people to hire for them. It produces information used for writing job descriptions (a list of what the job entails) and job specifications (what kind of people to hire for the job). The six steps of job analysis are: (1) Decide how the information will be used, since this determines the data to collect and how to collect them. (2) Review relevant background information such as organization charts, process charts and existing job descriptions. (3) Select representative positions, since there may be too many similar jobs to analyze. (4) Actually analyze the job by collecting data on job activities, required employee behaviors, working conditions, and human traits and abilities needed. (5) Verify the job analysis information with the worker performing the job and his or her immediate supervisor. (6) Develop a job description and job specification, the two tangible products of job analysis. Popular methods of collecting job analysis information are interviews, questionnaires, observations and diary/logs.

subjective.question: Describe the roles of employees and managers during the performance execution phase of PMS.
subjective.answer: Performance execution is the stage in which the performance to be evaluated is actually performed by employees according to the set standards and mutually decided goals. Employees' role: commitment to goal achievement (which is higher when goals are mutually set); sharing performance feedback with managers on an ongoing basis rather than delaying it till the review cycle; openly communicating about performance level and gaps with supervisors; collecting and sharing performance data accurately; and starting self-appraisals before the formal review by getting feedback from peers and customers. Managers' role: observation and documentation of performance for accurate, unbiased evaluation; updating employees about changes in goals, standards and preferences; providing continuous feedback so employees can improve before the formal review; providing the resources (equipment, machinery, growth opportunities) required to accomplish tasks; and reinforcement through rewards and encouragement so that positive feedback motivates future performance.

subjective.question: What is performance assessment? Discuss the role of multiple information sources and self-appraisal in it.
subjective.answer: Performance assessment is the phase of PMS in which the executed performance is evaluated by both employees (ratees) and managers (raters). Performance information can be gathered from multiple sources including supervisors, peers, customers and subordinates, although information provided by the supervisor is considered most important and is generally accepted. Using multiple sources ensures the accuracy of the PMS by reducing the chances of bias that may be high with a single source. Employees can also self-appraise their performance, which is beneficial for development purposes: the opportunity to self-assess enhances their trust level, satisfaction and perception regarding the fairness of PMS, so they openly accept the system. The active participation of both rater and ratee in this phase develops employee ownership of the performance rating and positively affects performance outcomes. However, self-appraisals are mostly highly rated compared to appraisals by others.

subjective.question: Differentiate between formal and informal performance review, and give recommendations for a productive performance review.
subjective.answer: An informal review takes place whenever a manager comments on a piece of work or an action of an employee to provide feedback, initiate coaching or show consensus on revised goals or corrective action; such meetings may not be formally documented unless action for poor performance is officially initiated. A formal review, usually known as an appraisal meeting, analyzes performance more systematically: it overviews performance since the last review, compares results with agreed performance standards, and its outcomes are formally documented on appraisal forms or employee files, assisting decisions about performance pay, promotion, demotion, development and training. Recommendations for a productive review: identify what the employee has done well and poorly with reference to displayed behavior; identify the factors behind performance from the employee's feedback and heed their explanations; give feedback in a positive manner and suggest improvement; identify the skills required to enhance performance; encourage employees to improve, incorporating their suggestions; and conduct follow-up meetings regularly to identify performance gaps timely.

subjective.question: What is performance renewal and re-contracting in the performance management process?
subjective.answer: Performance renewal and re-contracting is the last phase of PMS and is similar to the performance planning phase. In this phase, organizational goals, performance standards and desired behaviors are modified in accordance with the outcomes achieved in the previous phases. Considering these outcomes, the PM process is initiated again with the same phases while accommodating the outcomes of the previous cycle. In this manner PMS functions in a continuous manner: it is finalized in performance renewal and re-contracting, which initiates another cycle of PMS by redefining the prerequisites and performance planning.

subjective.question: Define strategic planning and state the steps involved in developing a strategic plan.
subjective.answer: Strategic planning is a process of defining organizational goals and strategies to attain those goals, allocating resources to implement plans, clarifying future prospects and continuously scanning the environment to identify opportunities and threats. It is a process of defining the organization's long-term goals and the tactics to achieve them. The steps to develop a strategic plan are: (1) Conduct an environmental analysis; (2) Develop organizational vision; (3) Craft organizational mission; (4) Set organizational goals; (5) Draft strategies to fulfill the mission and vision and achieve the goals.

subjective.question: What is environmental analysis? Explain the external and internal environment factors of an organization.
subjective.answer: Environmental analysis is a method to scan the environment of an organization to identify all the external and internal elements which can affect the organization's performance; the strategic planning process is initiated by environmental analysis. The external environment is composed of elements outside the organizational boundaries over which the organization has least or no control; it is a source of opportunities (components that help the organization succeed, e.g., government subsidies) and threats (factors that create difficulties and hinder success, e.g., imposed taxes, arrival of competitors, increasing inflation rates). Its factors include economy, political/legal, social, technological, competitors, customers and suppliers. The internal environment consists of factors in the direct control of the organization; its analysis identifies strengths (characteristics ensuring success) and weaknesses (characteristics hindering progress). Its components include organizational structure, organizational culture, organizational politics, processes and size.

subjective.question: What is gap analysis? Explain the four situations identified through gap analysis.
subjective.answer: Gap analysis is conducted on the basis of environmental analysis, which provides information about organizational strengths and weaknesses and the opportunities and threats in the surroundings; it responds to the external environment through internal abilities. The four situations are: (1) Opportunity + Strength = Leverage: an opportunity exists in the external environment and the organization has a related strength to take advantage of it; this is the ideal situation. (2) Opportunity + Weakness = Constraint: the environment offers an opportunity but the organization is internally not capable enough to avail it, an internally created constraint. (3) Threat + Strength = Vulnerability: the environment contains a threat but the organization has maintained successful operations due to its strengths; it remains vulnerable if it fails to retain those strengths. (4) Threat + Weakness = Problem: the worst situation, in which the organization is surrounded by external threats and is also internally weak; if sustained, it may lead to organizational decline or death.

subjective.question: Differentiate between mission, vision and goals of an organization.
subjective.answer: Mission: the mission statement describes the organization's aspirations in terms of who they are, what they do and the reason of their existence. An ideal mission statement illustrates the reason of organizational existence, scope of activities, customers and markets served, products and services offered, technology used, concern for growth or profitability, and the organization's values and beliefs. Vision: vision explains the future aspirations of the organization - what it wants to achieve in the long term; a vision statement should be brief, verifiable, bound by a timeline, focused on few specific areas, current, understandable and inspiring. Goals: after defining the broad mission and vision, specific goals are defined to facilitate their accomplishment; goals also serve as a source of motivation for employees, make the performance target tangible, and help in evaluating performance through attainment or non-attainment of the set goals. Goals are followed by strategies, which are broad at the organizational level and specific at the unit level.

subjective.question: What are performance standards? Give the characteristics of ideal performance standards and the process of developing them.
subjective.answer: A performance standard is a tool to ensure that performance will be up to the standard in a desirable, specified and observable manner; it evaluates performance in a quantifiable manner and describes the conditions that must exist before performance can be rated satisfactory. Standards communicate performance expectations among raters and ratees, and employee participation in defining them builds trust. Ideal performance standards should be measurable, observable, realistic and attainable. Performance is described in terms of required quantity, desired quality, timeliness, effective use of resources, effects of efforts, cooperation level, method of performing tasks and adjustment with organizational culture. The process of developing standards is: (1) Identify the top 3-5 primary job responsibilities of an employee; (2) Identify the performance indicators that will signify satisfactory performance of these responsibilities; (3) Identify the measurable and objective performance standards that reflect the minimum level of acceptable performance; (4) Identify the evaluation method, i.e., how the employee's performance of the responsibilities will be monitored. Pitfalls to avoid are ignoring individual efforts while assessing team performance, micromanagement (close supervision with no room for empowerment), and restricted dissemination of information about an employee's performance.

subjective.question: Explain the determinants of performance and their relationship with each other.
subjective.answer: The factors that cause the performance of an individual are called the determinants of performance: declarative knowledge, procedural knowledge and motivation. Declarative knowledge is based on factual information - information regarding the task's requirements, labels, principles and goals - and depicts the basic understanding of an employee regarding the job. Procedural knowledge is knowledge about the procedures to perform a task, i.e., what to do and how to do it, and depicts the employee's cognitive, physical, perceptual, motor and interpersonal skills. Motivation is a concept lying within or external to a person that energizes, directs and maintains behavior at the workplace; it involves the choice to perform, the level of effort and the persistence of effort. All three factors are essential and have a multiplicative relationship: Performance = Declarative Knowledge x Procedural Knowledge x Motivation. Hence if the value of any determinant is zero, performance will be zero; absence of any one factor leads to no performance.

subjective.question: Differentiate between task performance and contextual performance.
subjective.answer: Task performance focuses on the cognitive abilities of an individual and gives more emphasis to outcomes; its major concern is task accomplishment, considering the objective dimensions of performance. Contextual performance consists of volunteering activities that are not formally part of the job, such as suggesting organizational improvements, making constructive suggestions, assisting and helping coworkers and customers, respecting authority, and complying with organizational values and policies. The differences are: task performance varies across jobs while contextual performance is fairly similar across jobs; task performance is likely to be role prescribed while contextual performance is not; and the antecedents of task performance are abilities and skills, while the antecedents of contextual performance are personality. Both types should be included in evaluation, as both lead to organizational success.

subjective.question: Compare the trait, behavior and results approaches to measuring performance.
subjective.answer: Trait approach: it focuses on the individual through cognitive abilities and personality while ignoring the specific situation, behaviors and results. It is justified by the positive relationship between abilities/personality traits and desirable work behaviors, but it is criticized because traits are not under the control of individuals, are often God-gifted and relatively stable over the lifespan, and it cannot be ensured that particular traits lead to desired behaviors and results. Behavior approach: it emphasizes what employees do on the job; its main concern is behavior rather than traits or outcomes, and it is a process-oriented approach emphasizing how an employee performs the job regardless of the results attained. Results approach: it focuses on the outcomes produced by the employee. Behaviors and results are interrelated, but the link is not always obvious: desired results may not be achieved despite right behaviors (e.g., a salesperson unable to close a deal because of recession), and results may be achieved despite the absence of correct behaviors; therefore behaviors are mostly preferred for evaluation when the behavior-result link is weak.

subjective.question: What is poor performance? Discuss the internal and external factors that cause poor performance.
subjective.answer: An employee's performance is considered poor if it fails to meet the set performance standards of the organization. A performance problem refers to the discrepancy between expectations regarding work tasks and the actual tasks done. Internal factors are related to the performer and include lack of employee competence, low motivation and lack of confidence to accomplish the task. External factors lie outside the employee's influence. Organizational-level aspects include limited resources to facilitate job responsibilities, limited feedback about the task/job, weak reward-task link, unsupportive work culture and inadequate work systems. Social factors include corruption, lawlessness and a disabling environment. In order to deal with poor performance it is mandatory to diagnose its reasons: become aware of underperformance, identify the problem and assess its seriousness, identify the causes, decide and implement a solution, gather feedback on the implemented solution, and if nothing works, invoke a disciplinary procedure like a Performance Improvement Plan (PIP).

subjective.question: How can a manager deal with poor performance caused by a lack of ability and by low motivation?
subjective.answer: For lack of ability, there are five main ways, used in a sequence starting with the least intrusive: (1) Resupply - focus on the resources provided to do the job; ask employees about additional resources they need and verify their claims. (2) Retrain - provide additional training through seminars, computer-based training, simulation exercises or subsidized courses to keep skills current. (3) Refit - refit the job to the person by reassigning parts of the job and trying different combinations of tasks and abilities. (4) Reassign - reassign the poor performer to a role with reduced demands of responsibility, technical knowledge and interpersonal skills; demotion should never be used as a punishment tactic. (5) Release - as a final option, let the employee go when no reassignment opportunity exists and refitting is not appropriate. For low motivation, the three key interventions are: setting of performance goals (employees must understand and agree what they need to do to improve), provision of performance assistance (regularly assessing ability, providing training, securing resources, encouraging cooperation from coworkers), and provision of performance feedback (timely, open and honest feedback, with personalized rewards and recognition).

subjective.question: What are SMART goals? Explain each characteristic of a SMART goal.
subjective.answer: SMART goals are the organizational goals considered ideal and effective; SMART stands for Specific, Measurable, Attainable, Relevant and Time-bound. Specific: a specific goal has a much greater chance of being accomplished than a general goal; setting it requires clearing who is involved, what needs to be accomplished, where, when, which requirements and constraints apply, and why it is to be accomplished. Measurable: concrete criteria are established for measuring progress toward attainment of the goal, answering how much, how many, and how one will know when the goal is accomplished. Attainable: ways are figured out to make the goal come true by developing the attitudes, abilities, skills and financial capacity to reach it; a realistic goal represents an objective toward which employees are both willing and able to work. Relevant: the goal must be relevant to the purpose of the job and the achievement of the organization's mission and objectives. Time-bound (timely): the goal is grounded within a time frame, because with no time frame there is no sense of urgency.

subjective.question: Differentiate between threshold competencies and differentiating competencies.
subjective.answer: Threshold competencies depict the competence that everyone needs to display to do the job to a minimum standard; they do not distinguish high and low performers. For example, a management teacher should possess knowledge of the subject and the communication skills to effectively communicate it - this is the threshold competence without which he or she cannot perform effectively. Differentiating competencies distinguish between average and superior performers; they are a set of behavioral characteristics displayed by high performers. For example, a charismatic personality is a differentiating competence of a teacher, which motivates students, although the teacher can teach well even without possessing it.

subjective.question: Compare the comparative and absolute systems of measuring competencies, giving the methods of each.
subjective.answer: In comparative systems, an employee's competence level is evaluated by comparing it with other employees. Its methods are: simple rank order (employees ranked from best to worst), alternation rank order (best, then worst, then second best, then second worst, and so on), paired comparisons (each employee compared with every other; the number of pairs is n(n-1)/2), and forced distribution (employees apportioned according to an approximately normal distribution with a predefined quota). Comparative systems are easy to explain and control biases like leniency, strictness and average rating, but they usually evaluate on a single criterion, are relative and hence more likely to be legally challenged, and ranks do not measure the difference in performance. In absolute systems, employees are evaluated on the basis of their actual performance regardless of any comparison with other performers. Its methods are essays, behavior checklist, critical incidents, graphic rating scales and Behaviorally Anchored Rating Scales (BARS).

subjective.question: What are appraisal forms? Discuss the components of an appraisal form and the features that make it effective.
subjective.answer: An appraisal form is an instrument used to collect information on employee performance, on the basis of which performance is evaluated; it is also used to document performance and maintain the record, and can be filled manually or electronically. Its components are: (1) Basic employee information (job title, division, employee number, pay scale, evaluation period dates, etc.); (2) Accountabilities, objectives and standards; (3) Competencies and indicators; (4) Major achievements and contributions; (5) Developmental achievements; (6) Developmental needs, plans and goals; (7) Stakeholder input (from customers, peers and subordinates); (8) Employee's comments; and (9) Signatures of the ratee, rater and rater's supervisor. The desirable features that make a form effective include simplicity, relevancy, descriptiveness, adaptability, comprehensiveness, definitional clarity, communication and time orientation (addressing both past and future performance).
